outliers.why: Only design that makes licence jurisdiction the literal first path segment (units/<imprint>/<slug>) while simultaneously banning ALL machine-generated bytes from VCS and routing them to an external immutable artefact registry with provenance — the most extreme 'nothing generated is ever tracked' + 'rights are physically load-bearing' combination in the draw, yet fully coherent (0 forced fits, self-score 29, explicit trajectory reasoning for keeping status independent of role).

The only design where the repository boundary itself carries the primary classification with just four axes (License class, Stability guarantee, Change rhythm, Reusability boundary) — the lowest cardinality among all repo-splitting proposals and structurally the most 'physically enforced, semantically thin' of the multi-repo family (~8 repos), deliberately rejecting richer per-unit metadata in favour of hard filesystem/repo segregation.

Persona (registry operator) plus a 'no lifecycle/clock concept' constraint produced pure package-registry vocabulary (kind, dependencyClass, byteAuthority, reuseGrant, carriage, stewardship) with a closed R0-R4/D dependency-rank matrix and zero forced fits across all 20 probes — the most mechanically strict, zero-ambiguity manifest system in the draw, markedly more registry-native than any other single-repo design.

shortfalls: Only one reportable event across all 46 records: walker 0 (crossVendor grounding) self-declared an accidental exposure — a broad path-only manifest search surfaced directory names beneath .claude/worktrees/, including one containing "census" and the existing study-parent directory name containing "deconstruction"; no file body was opened, no prohibited or out-of-repo path was read, nothing was written, and the surfaced names did not inform the proposal. This is a benign self-report, not a violation.
No cross-vendor failures were reported by any of the crossVendor:true walkers (idx 0, 8, 16, 24, 32) — all completed with substantive, scored proposals.

No empty or null results anywhere in the batch — every walker produced a full descriptor set, layout sketch, probe classifications, trajectory, and self-scores; several (idx 34, 37, 38) simply returned an empty rubricEscapes array with no other omission.

archive.diversityNote: Genuine divergence was constraint-driven, not persona-driven. Of the 46 usable records, 19 (41%) landed in one dominant cell — a 5-6 axis classification carried by a role/tier directory family with generated bytes committed to VCS — regardless of whether the persona was a librarian, taxonomist, zoning planner, or naval architect; persona vocabulary changed (Substance Type vs UNIT-TYPE vs Purpose Class) but the underlying descriptor tuple did not. A further 5 walkers reproduced the identical shape at higher cardinality (7-8, forced by the exactly-seven constraint) and 3 at lower cardinality (2, forced by the exactly-two constraint) — so even the "different cardinality" cells are the same family-carrier architecture wearing a constraint-sized coat. Real structural divergence appeared only where the injected constraint made the default answer impossible: "layout at most one level deep" produced a genuine flat/naming-prefix family (4 walkers), "nothing may be renamed or moved" produced a genuine metadata-only-over-existing-layout family (4 walkers), "split into two or more repositories" produced actual multi-repo designs (3 walkers), and "machine-generated artefacts may not live in VCS" produced a coherent no-VCS-generated family (5 walkers, split across two carrier styles: zone-directory and flat-manifest). Grounding mode (repo-direct vs facts-sheet vs requirements-only) and crossVendor flag showed no visible effect on descriptor shape — the facts-sheet and requirements-only walkers converged onto the same dominant cell as repo-direct walkers just as often. So the walkers did explore real alternative organisational grammars, but only six or seven of them, not forty-six — the apparent diversity of 46 distinct proposals compresses to roughly a dozen architecturally distinct cells, most of them forced open by the constraint rather than discovered by the persona.

scorerObservations: Systemic weak spot shared by nearly every cell: P3 (byte-preserved third-party files adjacent to hand-written styling) is almost universally split along provenance/licence lines, directly against the measured 85% co-change between 'byte-preserved capture and styling code' — the single most consistent boundary-fitness defect in the archive.

The dominant convergence shape (19/46 walkers, exemplified by elite walker 35) routes pipeline source to a code/ tree and its regenerated output to a separate data/ or generated/ tree, severing the codegen pipeline's 95%/89%/86% internal co-change pairs across the modal architecture of the whole draw, not just isolated cells — this is an archive-wide risk, not a per-walker quirk.

No proposal in the reviewed set differentiates the typed client's agent-tool layer (117 commits, only 32% co-change with the client remainder — a confirmed independent cluster) from the rest of the client; S4 is treated as one atomic package everywhere it appears, so the single most load-bearing 'independent cluster' number in the measured record goes unaddressed by every elite.

Repository-boundary designs pay the steepest boundary-fitness cost when they split a high-coupling pair, since a repo crossing is a release-and-migrate event, not a directory move: walker 8 pays this against the pipeline's highest coupling (95%, mining workflow vs. its corpus), while walker 44, under the same constraint, avoids it by keeping type-generation and all four generated-artefact collections in one repo.

Multiple archive summary fields don't reconcile with the underlying walker data on recount: eliteForcedFits for walkers 0, 4, 7, and 21, and eliteSelfScoreSum for walkers 16, 21, and 45, plus the walker-40 outlier blurb's '0 forced fits' claim. These look like archive-compilation errors rather than walker misreporting; round 2 should re-derive both fields from each walker's own probeClassifications and selfScores rather than propagate the cell/outlier summaries as given.

draw.constraint: no lifecycle or clock concept is permitted anywhere in your design

designQuestions: What coherent work does this unit represent, and what is explicitly outside it?
What stable name identifies it?
On which shelf does it live?
Which unit relations are permitted: import, execute, consume, produce, embed?
Which byte sets are authored, generated, or preserved?
Who may edit or approve each byte set?
What rights attach to each byte set and what notices travel with it?
Which quality, publication, and deployment rules apply?
What graph and configuration changes follow from reorganising it?

classifications.name: Identity
classifications.question: What stable ID, name, scope, audience, and subject identify this unit?
classifications.values: Stable kebab-case unit-id; package name @oaknational/<unit-id>; banned vague names (shared, common, core, utils)
classifications.carrier: manifest field — colocated units/<role>/<id>/unit.json (after revision step 2; v0 was a central catalogue)

classifications.name: Role
classifications.question: What kind of work is this, determining its shelf and relation ceiling?
classifications.values: foundation, capability, client, adapter, generator, product, demonstration, tool, study, collection, estate
classifications.carrier: layout level — units/<role>/ shelf, plus the unit.json record

classifications.name: Relations
classifications.question: Who may import, execute, consume, produce, or embed whom?
classifications.values: declared imports, public exports, byte consumption, production, embedding, execution; role ceilings plus per-unit allowlists
classifications.carrier: manifest field (unit.json + package.json exports) enforced via generated dependency-graph/ESLint config

classifications.name: editAuthority
classifications.question: Who may edit or approve each byte set?
classifications.values: named editor/approver groups per glob (e.g. curator, brand-steward)
classifications.carrier: manifest field in unit.json plus generated CODEOWNERS sections (split from Custody in revision step 1)

classifications.name: derivation
classifications.question: Are these bytes authored, generated, or preserved, and what regenerates them?
classifications.values: authored | generated (with declared producer, inputs, outputs) | preserved (hash-locked)
classifications.carrier: manifest field plus provenance.lock.json hashes and generated-file headers (split from Custody in revision step 1)

classifications.name: Rights
classifications.question: Under what licence may each byte set travel or be reused?
classifications.values: SPDX expression or named restricted-rights reference per glob (MIT, content licence, LicenseRef-Oak-Trademark, third-party)
classifications.carrier: manifest field per glob plus travelling LICENCES.md/NOTICE files

classifications.name: Assurance
classifications.question: Which quality gates, publication rules, and deployment eligibility apply?
classifications.values: gate set; public/private publication; production-deployment eligibility (demonstrations ineligible)
classifications.carrier: enforcement rule — unit.json field driving generated gate configuration, checked by pnpm organisation:check

result.layoutSketch:
units/
  foundations/<unit-id>/   (result, path-safety, graph-data)
  capabilities/<unit-id>/  (design-system, search-store-contract, curriculum-search-retrieval, curriculum-widget)
  clients/<unit-id>/       (curriculum-api)
  adapters/<unit-id>/      (elasticsearch-search-store, elasticsearch-retrieval, sentry-observability)
  generators/<unit-id>/    (design-tokens, curriculum-api-acquisition, curriculum-types, curriculum-data-mining)
  products/<unit-id>/      (curriculum-mcp-service)
  demonstrations/<unit-id>/ (curriculum-hub)
  tools/<unit-id>/         (repository-policy, agent-coordination, analysis-automation, delivery-automation)
  studies/<unit-id>/       (web-app-evidence)
  collections/<unit-id>/   (curriculum-api-spec, curriculum-bulk-data, design-source-capture, curriculum-reference-data, oak-brand-assets, curriculum-search-vocabulary)

Each leaf: unit.json (authoritative seven-facet record), package.json exports, src/index.ts + declared subpaths, provenance.lock.json, LICENCES.md/NOTICE. Root: estate-root unit owning root config; generated catalogue.json + CATALOGUE.md finding aids; one closed organisation.schema.json; single pnpm organisation:check enforcing ownership, boundaries, regeneration, hashes, rights, and demonstration/production separation. Separateness rule: a separate unit exists only when a nameable coherent work needs an independent contract, dependency prohibition, rights/edit-authority boundary, or assurance class — format, file count, producer mechanism, or shared external source never suffice alone.

designQuestions: What makes two things SEPARATE units? Different refresh rhythms (external schedule vs hand curation), different licence classes that cannot mix, or different access patterns (product-runtime vs tooling-only). Structural separation via directory zones.

WHERE does a unit live and how does a newcomer find it? Location encodes identity—/packages/platform for libraries, /packages/products for deployed code, /src/pipeline for hand-curated generation, /content for licence-incompatible reference, /spec-cache for machine-generated, /assets for brand-reserved.

Who may IMPORT whom? Licence zones are firewall boundaries; refresh-velocity isolation means machine-generated never directly imported at source. Products cannot import from each other. Encoding in ESLint rules and .gitignore.

Who may EDIT which bytes, and what regenerates machine-produced ones? File directory and suffix encode edit authority—/src/pipeline/hand-curated is human-editable, /spec-cache and generated subdirs are CI-regenerated. Enforcement via .gitignore and pre-commit hooks.

Under what LICENCE does each unit travel or get reused? Directory zones encode licence class—/packages and /src are permissive code only, /content is OGL-licensed (never exported), /assets is brand-reserved, /research is internal-only. Import rules prevent licence-incompatible mixing.

What is the cost to CHANGE the organisation itself later? Adding new refresh-velocity class needs directory zone + ESLint rule (~2-3 files). Moving unit between zones is cheap (rename + update imports). Restructuring products is expensive (affects 20+ import paths).

classifications.carrier: Directory zone (/src vs /spec-cache vs /content) + file suffix (.generated.ts vs .manual.ts) + .gitignore policy

classifications.name: LICENCE_SPHERE

selfScores.evidence: Answerability: agents can answer all 6 decision needs by directory path alone, no README scanning needed. Carrier: 5 classifications, each maps to one carrier (directory zone, suffix, eslint rule, package.json metadata). Agent economics: globs like /packages/products/*, /packages/platform/*, /src/pipeline/* are obvious. Change robustness: adding new refresh-velocity class costs 2-3 files (directory, eslint, .gitignore); moving unit is cheap (rename + imports); restructuring products is expensive (20+ imports). selfScores.evidence: Answerability: Six decision questions answered directly; layout = directory path makes finding units obvious (ask 'which /packages/X does this belong in?'). Carrier Economy: Five carriers (layout, manifest, depcruise, workflow, CI gates) is reasonable; two involve human discipline (ds-bundle read-only culture, package.json private flag), but both are documented and CI-visible. designQuestions: What makes two things separate units? — Physical boundary (package.json), edit ownership (hand vs machine), change rhythm (source vs fetched vs generated), and import flow (what imports what). Separation is justified when any of these differ.

Where does a unit live and how does a newcomer find it? — Location encodes purpose: packages/[zone]/[unit] where zone signals dependency level (core → libs → sdks → apps). Discovery via npm namespace @oaknational/[name]. Zones: Core (primitives, zero-deps), Libs (integration, depends on core), SDKs (surface, depends on core+libs), Design (independent tree), Apps (deployed), Demos (not product), Ops (agent-tools substrate), Research (evidence code), Reference (curated data).

Who may import whom, and in what direction? — Strict layering: core imports nothing; libs import core; sdks import core+libs; apps import anything below. Design is independent. Agent-tools reads repos as data (no code imports). Enforcement via depcruise rules (graph-level) and ESLint boundaries (per-file).

Who may edit which bytes, and what regenerates machine-produced ones? — Source files (src/*.ts) are hand-authored. Machine-produced bytes live in dist/, src/types/generated/, and marked generated directories. Regeneration is idempotent; validators enforce byte parity post-rebuild. Edit ownership is unambiguous: source directory vs generated directory.

Under what licence each unit may travel? — MIT for all source code (packages/core, libs, sdks, apps). OGL for hand-curated reference data (ground-truths/). Brand-reserved for trademark assets (oak-design-assets/). Generated artefacts inherit parent licence. Scope is per-package, declared in package.json.

What does it cost to change the organisation later? — Moving a package up-level (lib→sdk) requires reviewing and updating importers; breaks stability. Splitting a package requires coordinating all workspace members and updating imports. Changing reference-data licence scope requires auditing consumers. Reorganising zones is low-cost (directory rename); reorganising *into* zones is higher (import path updates). No moving-target surfaces; costs are visible.

selfScores.evidence: Answerability: Each of the 6 design needs is answered with explicit, spatially verifiable reasoning (zones encode purpose; licence scope is per-package; import rules are written depcruise rules live in the codebase). Enforcement: depcruise rules and ESLint boundaries are active in CI (not aspirational); byte-parity validators are working code. Carrier: Most classifications use directory structure and package.json (spatial, unambiguous); regeneration triggers require reading build config (not purely spatial). Agent: Path to unit is spatial (packages/[zone]/[unit]); path to rebuild trigger requires config knowledge (implicit, not spatial). Change robustness: Moving packages is visible cost (imports break, depcruise fails); no hidden costs. Splitting is coordinated (workspace update required). Migration: Current structure is 95% compliant; ratification needs licence declarations and P3 validation enforcement, not reshuffling. Both are forward additions, no breaking changes.

draw.constraint: every rule in your design must be machine-checkable, or you must discard the rule

designQuestions: What makes two things SEPARATE units? Two things belong in different units when they differ in: license class (MIT, OGL, brand-reserved), regeneration ownership model (human-edited vs machine-generated-by-process-X), shipped vs internal status, or import visibility. Within zones, responsibility domain creates sub-units.

WHERE does a unit live, and how does a newcomer find it? Directory path encodes the conflict class (zone): /specs (generated specs), /data (generated data), /app (product server), /cli (tools), /ui (applications), /libs/public (public APIs), /libs/internal (internal code), /content (reference content), /reference (demos), /brand (assets), /tools (internal tooling), /research (evidence), /scripts (ops). Newcomers navigate by (1) license class → zone, (2) responsibility → sub-path.

Who may IMPORT whom? Acyclic graph within each zone. Generated artifacts (/specs/*, /data/*) can be imported by anywhere. Cross-zone imports: content↔code blocked by license (ESLint), tools→runtime blocked by ownership (Turbo visibility), research only consumed by research. Within Product Code: /libs/internal and /libs/public can be imported by /app, /cli, /ui but not vice versa.

Who may EDIT which bytes, and what regenerates automatically? Each zone has explicit ownership: /specs, /data/bulk, /data/generated: read-only, regenerated by CI triggers (spec-fetch, data-fetch, index-build). /app, /cli, /ui, /libs: human-edited via PR. /content, /reference: human-edited with content review. /brand: owner-only. /tools: internal-team edited. /research: research-team edited. Regenerated bytes never hand-edited; changes happen in source (config, external API) and trigger rebuild.

Under what LICENSE may each unit travel? /app, /cli, /ui: MIT (or chosen open license). /libs/public: MIT. /libs/internal: internal (not published). /content, /reference: OGL 3.0 (or content license). /brand: brand-reserved/trademark. /tools: MIT, internal-only. /research: research-specific license. /specs, /data: derived from source (often restrictive). Cross-zone imports fail CI: content→code and code→content blocked by ESLint no-restricted-imports rule.

What's the cost of CHANGING the organisation itself later? Reorganizing within a zone is cheap (move files, update imports, regenerate if needed). Reorganizing ACROSS zones is expensive: license reclassification, ownership transfer, publishing decisions. Splitting a unit: need explicit API boundary agreement and test coverage. Merging units: unify quality gates and licensing. The zone boundary itself is the cost lever; moving something from zone X to zone Y requires explicit decision and review. Estimated migration effort for current estate: moderate for product code, high for generated artifacts, very high for mixed-license files.

trajectory.perturbation: Move demo applications from /ui/demo-* (Shipped Product Code zone) to /reference/demo-* (Reference Material zone) — rationale: demos are reference material, not shipped product code. Prevents accidental inclusion in deployed product.
trajectory.why: KEPT: Demos are not product and do not belong in the product-code zone. This move (1) makes intent explicit, (2) prevents cognitive load (developers no longer wonder 'is this shipped?'), (3) enables stricter import rules (product can't import reference), (4) isolates demo-specific dependencies from product. Directly satisfies P9 and improves answerability of 'what makes units separate'.

trajectory.perturbation: Split /libs/public and /libs/internal into separate pnpm workspaces with independent CI pipelines — rationale: public APIs require SemVer, backwards compatibility, deprecation policy; internal code can evolve freely. Result: different package.json, different test/lint/build tasks.
trajectory.why: KEPT: Versioning and publishing discipline MUST be separate. Public libraries (S4: curriculum client) need strict stability rules; internal libraries (S1-S3) can evolve freely without breaking external consumers. This split (1) makes governance boundaries explicit, (2) reduces cost of later publishing decisions (S3 can be promoted to public cleanly), (3) allows different CI cadence and quality gates. Improves changeRobustness and enforcementHonesty.

selfScores.evidence: Answerability (4/5): Design gives explicit criteria (license, ownership, shipped-ness, visibility) for separation, but 'responsibility domain' is somewhat subjective. Enforcement (5/5): Every rule has machine-checkable carrier (ESLint, GitHub Actions, package.json, CODEOWNERS). Carrier economy (4/5): Directory structure, package.json, ESLint, GitHub Actions, CODEOWNERS cover most; credential isolation carrier not fully specified. Agent economics (5/5): Directory-based zones navigable via glob; README at zone roots explains boundaries; import rules prevent accidental cross-zone pollution. Change robustness (4/5): Within-zone reorganization cheap; cross-zone expensive but intentional; big multi-zone refactors not fully accounted. Migration realism (3/5): Clear design, but actual migration of 10,800 files requires (1) identifying current ownership, (2) re-licensing mixed files, (3) splitting monolithic packages, (4) updating CI — moderate-to-high coordination cost, no blockers.

rubricEscapes: No critical escapes: design answers all 6 decision questions. Future considerations (out of scope): SemVer and deprecation policy for public libraries (S4); credential rotation and access control for external services (curriculum API); build-time impact and caching strategy for generated artifacts (P1, P2); compliance and audit procedures for government-licensed content (P5).

draw.constraint: your design must rest on exactly seven independent classifications

designQuestions: What makes two things a separate unit rather than part of one?
Where does a unit live in the filesystem, and how does a human or agent discover it?
Who may import whom — what dependency rules govern the import graph?
Who may edit which bytes, and what is machine-regenerated versus hand-written?
Under what legal terms may each unit travel, and what licenses must never mix in one unit?
What does it cost to reorganize this structure later, and what creates coupling that prevents easy reorganization?

selfScores.evidence: Answerability (4/5): All six questions have clear metadata answers (package.json, path, rules, .gitignore), navigable by a tool. One deduction: CHANGE_RHYTHM requires reading multiple carriers (scripts + src structure + gitignore patterns); a consolidated generate-manifest field would improve to 5/5. Enforcement (5/5): Path-based + package.json + dependency-cruiser rules + git hooks + CI/CD config make every classification mechanically auditable; zero human judgment required. Carrier economy (4/5): Learn 4-5 carrier types (package.json fields, path location, .gitignore, dependency-cruiser rules). A normalized generate-manifest field in package.json would centralize dispersed build config signals; with that, 5/5. Agent economics (5/5): No paths move or rename; renames forbidden by design. All change is metadata deltas: description updates, rule updates, private flag flips. Reorg cost is bounded by config changes, not structural surgery. Change robustness (5/5): Metadata-only org survives any classification shift without structural moves. New asset class (e.g., ML models) requires new UNIT_KIND value, but schema is expressive for classes seen so far. Migration (4/5): Adoption is 10 hours (assign UNIT_KIND, formalize CHANGE_RHYTHM via src, encode IMPORT_CEILING in rules, add CONTENT_LICENCE, document EDITION_CONTROL, formalize DEPLOYMENT_RHYTHM). Ongoing: linter enforces every classification. One deduction: team discipline to keep descriptions accurate; a lint rule checking UNIT_KIND against path location would reduce drift. With that, 5/5.

result.layoutSketch: Flat stable-ID layout: units/<unit-id>/ (e.g. units/core.errors/, units/curriculum.api-client/, units/repo.integrity/, units/search.retrieval/), each with a hand-authored unit.yaml material passport carrying contract, legal, custody, lifecycle, purpose, exposure. Names are <domain>.<capability>[.<facet>], never team names; proper nouns only where a supplier/vendor boundary is the point. Purpose and exposure are manifest fields, not path levels. Generated payloads never live in Git: they go to content-addressed artifact storage / package registry / ignored read-only materialisation dirs, consumed via declared typed artifact edges. Supply-chain flow: supplier input -> acquisition unit (quarantine, licence/integrity checks) -> immutable input lot in CAS -> transformation unit on read-only checkout -> immutable generated lot + provenance attestation -> declared artifact edge to consumers. Import rules: no cross-unit relative imports; explicit typed acyclic edge graph; products/demos never importable; commodity vendors behind ports with adapters; lockfiles also live in protected artifact storage keyed by digest of authored dependency intent.

selfScores.evidence: (1) Separation: 5/5 — five independent classifications provide unambiguous split logic for every probe; no ambiguity. (2) Findability: 5/5 — deterministic three-question path (licence→service→consumer) is learnable and machine-navigable. (3) Imports: 4/5 — licence segregation and editability rules are clear and sufficient for most cases; edge cases require judgment. (4) Editability: 5/5 — explicit classification; regeneration sources traceable; machine-produced code is never ambiguous. (5) Licence: 5/5 — hard root-level segregation; three classes never mix by design; visibility at first path component. (6) Change cost: 4/5 — scaling model is sound (new services→new roots, new consumers→subdirs, five classifications stable); typical costs not quantified numerically. Agent economics (4/5): three-to-five levels of nesting is navigable for LLMs; could flatten further, but trade-off with clarity is acceptable. Migration realism (4/5): within-root moves are cheap; cross-root moves rare and expensive, which is desirable constraint.

designQuestions: What makes two things separate units of code? Answer: Distinct combination of reusability scope (public/internal/private), publication/licensing boundary, change rhythm, team ownership authority, and deployment/versioning independence.

Where does a unit live and how does a newcomer (human or AI) find the right one? Answer: Three-tier hierarchy {layer}/{concern}/{unit}, navigable top-down: layer (packages/apps/demos/agent-tools/research) determines function, concern (core/libs/sdks/design/platform/product) determines governance, unit name is specific.

Who may import whom? Answer: Unidirectional dependency: core ← libs ← sdks ← apps/demos. Design and agent-tools are independent (no code deps). Research is isolated. Enforced at four levels: directory structure, package.json exports, ESLint rules, and depcruise configuration.

Who may edit which bytes, and what regenerates machine-produced ones? Answer: Hand-authored code in src/, generated/cached in src/generated/ or .generated/, bulk-fetched data in .data/. Regeneration is explicit (CLI command, scheduled job, or build step). Pre-commit hook prevents accidental edits to marked generated files.

Under what license does each unit travel or get reused? Answer: Code defaults to MIT. Content/data is OGL v3.0 (from upstream API). Assets are reserved (Oak brand). Mixed units declare all applicable licenses in package.json and README. License compliance is checked in CI.

What does it cost to change the organisation itself? Answer: Within-layer directory moves are low-cost (rename only). Unit splits are medium-cost (consumers need updates). Tier boundary changes are high-cost (dependency inversions). Organisational restructures are very high-cost (team boundary changes). Mitigation: keep boundaries shallow, enforce rules via machines not vigilance.

designQuestions: What makes two code units separate (not merged together)?
Where does a unit live and how does a newcomer find the right one?
What import rules govern which units may depend on which others?
Who may edit which bytes, and what regenerates machine-produced code?

classifications.name: License Class
classifications.question: Can these two units share a directory or inherit rules from a common parent?
classifications.values: Permissive-Code (MIT or equivalent), Government-Licensed-Content (OGL, cannot mix with code), Trademark-Reserved (different reuse model, isolated)
classifications.carrier: Directory location (apps/, packages/, tools/, .infrastructure/, reference/, content/, brand/) + LICENSE file at unit root

classifications.name: Refresh Source & Ownership
classifications.question: How often does this unit change, who decides when, and what triggers the change?
classifications.values: Hand-Curated (humans decide, version-controlled), Machine-Generated (external event or build triggers, never hand-edit), External-Spec-Driven (API snapshot refresh ~29x/yr), Bulk-Fetch-Driven (bulk data refresh ~7x/yr), Hand-Written-Code (human changes, no machine regeneration)
classifications.carrier: Directory (generated/ vs packages/ vs content/) + regeneration.ts file in each generated unit mapping triggers per module

classifications.name: Edit Policy
classifications.question: May humans hand-edit the bytes in this unit?
classifications.values: Never (machine-generated, pre-commit hook blocks edits), Always (hand-written code), Constrained (hand-curated reference data, edit in version-control only), Append-Only (logs, data stores)
classifications.carrier: package.json field `generated: true` (for generated/) + pre-commit hook + lint enforcement

classifications.name: Import Scope
classifications.question: Who in the estate may import this unit's public API?
classifications.values: Anywhere (utility primitives), Products-Only (product-specific), Libraries-Only (infrastructure only), Workforce-Only (build/commit time), Internal-Only (hidden behind adapter)
classifications.carrier: eslint-plugin-boundaries rules OR package.json exports field, documented in unit README

classifications.name: Regeneration Trigger
classifications.question: Under what condition does this unit rebuild or refresh?
classifications.values: External-API-Change (curriculum spec snapshot ~29x/yr), Build-Event (types ~29x/yr, search contracts ~16x/yr), Commit-Event (hooks), Bulk-Fetch-Driven (schemas ~7x/yr, corpus ~19x/yr), Search-Index-Change, Manual-Command, Never (hand-written)
classifications.carrier: regeneration.ts (mapping module → [triggers]) in each generated/ unit, documented in README

classifications.name: Audience
classifications.question: Who is the primary consumer of this unit?
classifications.values: End-Users (delivered products), AI-Agents (curriculum server, search CLI), Workforce (validators, hooks, tooling), Products (internal platform code), Content-Platform-Users (curriculum via API)
classifications.carrier: README and documentation + directory grouping

result.layoutSketch:
Flat single-level directory structure at monorepo root, organized by audience and license class:

├─ apps/  Runnable products (curriculum-server, search-cli, demo-pages, widget-builder)
├─ packages/  Reusable libraries (lib-error, lib-path-safety, lib-graph, client-curriculum, lib-search, spec-acquisition, vocab-curation, pipeline-generation, search-datastore-adapter, observability-adapter, design-tokens)
├─ tools/  Workforce tooling (validators, hooks, workspace-config, session-tools, ops-scripts)
├─ generated/  Machine-produced code with unified namespace + module-level triggers (specs/, schemas/, types/, index/, corpus/, widget/, vendored/)
├─ content/  Government-licensed curriculum reference data (curriculum-reference/)
├─ brand/  Trademark assets (assets/, guidelines/)
├─ reference/  Research & examples (research/, examples/)
└─ .infrastructure/  Monorepo machinery (config/, scripts/)

Within each top-level directory: one semantic unit name per directory, with clear package.json, src/, and README. No further nesting. Glob patterns are predictable (e.g., apps/*, packages/*, tools/*, generated/*/). License and edit policy declared at unit root."

trajectory.perturbation: Merge generated/ sub-directories into unified namespace with module-level trigger configs
trajectory.why: All generated code shares edit policy (never hand-edit) and license inheritance. Merging reduces unit count and simplifies import graph (one generated dependency instead of many). Regeneration complexity stays, moves inside via regeneration.ts config. Acceptable trade-off: less unit discovery overhead, same expressiveness.

trajectory.perturbation: Split tools/ by edit policy: machine-generated hooks to generated/hooks/, hand-written validators to tools/validators/
trajectory.why: Hooks are fundamentally tools (build/commit-time machinery) even though non-editable. Placing in generated/ violates semantic category. Better to keep hooks in tools/, mark generated: true in package.json, enforce via pre-commit hook. Semantic category stronger than edit-policy difference.

trajectory.perturbation: Split S7 (generation pipeline, ~600 commits/yr) into five units by classification: spec-acquisition (library), vocab-curation (library), pipeline-generation (orchestration), generated/types (machine), generated/corpus (machine)
trajectory.why: Different edit policies (hand vs machine), different refresh triggers (~29x types, ~19x corpus), different dependencies justify separation. Coupling between units is documented in triggers and README. Enables independent work; surfaces real boundaries currently hidden. Complexity acceptable given boundaries are clear.

selfScores.evidence: Design fully answers all six needs via six independent classifications, each with a concrete carrier (directory structure, package.json flags, regeneration.ts configs, enforcement rules). Enforcement is achievable via directory globs + pre-commit hooks + eslint-plugin-boundaries (not purely structural, requires tooling). Carriers are economic (directory broadcasts intent; package.json and trigger-configs hold detail). Agent navigation works via flat structure + glob patterns + semantic names. Change robustness is limited at top level (directory renaming is high-cost), but adding units is low-cost. Migration is realistic via gradual adoption (new code follows structure, old code migrates incrementally). Only minor gap: P7 (research code) has no natural home and is forced into reference/ as catch-all.

designQuestions: What makes two code units separate organizational units (not sub-folders within a larger unit)?

classifications.name: Provenance
classifications.question: Source of truth and control model: how does the code come to exist and who edits it?
classifications.values: Authored (hand-written, version-controlled by contributors) | Derived (generated from upstream source-of-truth, regenerated on updates, never hand-edited) | Ingested (third-party source, byte-preserved, never locally edited)
classifications.carrier: Directory layout (/packages/foundation/ vs /packages/generated/ vs /packages/third-party/) + .gitignore rules (Derived outputs ignored or committed read-only) + naming conventions (generated code suffixed or marked in package.json)

classifications.name: Layer
classifications.question: Scope and dependency position: what is this unit for and who imports it?
classifications.values: Foundation (infrastructure, primitives, core utilities — widely-imported by many units, bottom of dependency stack) | Vertical (product-specific code, domain logic, business logic tied to one product or domain) | Attached (tooling, support, research, demonstrations — operational, never imported by core product code, lower quality bar on research itself)
classifications.carrier: Directory structure (/packages/foundation/ /apps/ /tools/ /research/) + import rules enforced by linter (dependency-cruiser) + package naming (@oaknational/X vs @oaknational/X-tool vs @oaknational/X-research)

trajectory.perturbation: Add naming suffix convention: -tool, -support, -generated to mark Attachment or Provenance status in every import
trajectory.why: Strengthens findability (Q2). Naming makes governance visible: import from '@oaknational/X-tool' immediately signals lower quality bar. Supports Q4 (edit rules) and Q3 (import rules) via convention.

selfScores.evidence: Answerability: 4 — two classifications answer all six questions clearly, but Q6 (cost of change) needs explicit versioning strategy, not just org design. Enforcement: 5 — Provenance checked at build (regenerate outputs, never commit hand-edits); Layer checked by dependency linter. Carrier economy: 5 — lightweight: filesystem structure + .gitignore + naming suffixes. Agent economics: 4 — two classification questions are answerable (authored vs generated? infrastructure vs product?), but Vertical vs Foundation boundary sometimes blurs (domain-specific lib vs shared lib). Change robustness: 3 — stable for new units, costly to reorganize existing ones. Migration: 4 — most units already in right places; P10 needs extraction, P3 needs decomposition, agent-tools needs partitioning.

rubricEscapes: Build and distribution versioning: how do Derived units version independently from their upstream source? (e.g., design tokens version separately from Oak design system) — organizational design says regenerated but doesn't address versioning rhythm.

Third-party sync and update rhythm: when an Ingested asset is updated (major version bump), what's the update cadence and communication? Design says never-edit-locally but not transitive dependency management.

Transitive Provenance risk: can an Authored unit safely depend on a Derived unit that depends on an Ingested unit from an unstable vendor API? Design doesn't address depth limits or transitive provenance tracking.

Quality-gate variance enforcement: Attached units have lower quality bars. When does Attached code quality affect a Vertical product that imports it? Design specifies the Layer difference but not the quality boundary enforcement.

classifications.name: Tier
classifications.question: What direction may imports flow?
classifications.values: Foundation (universal primitives, ~0 deps) | Platform (shared infra, crosses domains) | Application (end-user-facing, imports downward)

classifications.values: Shipped (reaches end users, strict semver) | EcosystemAPI (external SDK, version-pinned) | Internal (workforce + internal APIs, can break with notice) | Unshipped (demo or research, gated or experimental)
classifications.carrier: package.json private flag (Internal/Unshipped); separate build targets; tsconfig include/exclude; publishing step filters

classifications.name: Refresh Cadence
classifications.question: How often do changes force rebuilds of dependents?
classifications.values: Stable (≤4 times/year, e.g., spec snapshots, brand assets) | Moderate (10-15x/year, e.g., search contracts, design tokens) | Frequent (weekly or on-commit, e.g., generated types, CI tools) | OnDemand (manual trigger or external event, e.g., widget rebuild)
classifications.carrier: Turbo cache rules (stable = longer cache TTL); GitHub Actions trigger frequency; dependency bounds version constraints; monorepo task scheduling

trajectory.why: Merging Editability loses enforcement distinction: Preserved files need .gitignore rules to prevent accidental edits; Generated files need build regeneration scripts. Same Cadence value doesn't imply same enforcement mechanism. Splitting Tier is theoretically elegant but doesn't improve org design—Infrastructure vs. Domain describes a deployment concern, not a structural one. Rejected to preserve enforcement fidelity.

trajectory.perturbation: Split Audience 'PublicAPI' into two: EcosystemAPI (external SDK consumers, version-pinned, e.g., S4) vs. Internal-published (internal published APIs, can break with notice, e.g., S3). Clarifies versioning SLA and governance cost.
trajectory.why: Improves clarity and responsibility. External SDK changes require deprecation cycles and major-version bumps for external consumers. Internal-published changes only need internal coordination. Cost: adds one directory level (e.g., /packages/code/platform/ecosystem/curriculum-client). Enforcement: build system can block Ecosystem units from importing Internal-published ones. Clarity gained justifies the cost.

trajectory.perturbation: Move /scripts/ (P8, ops scripts) into /tools/ungated-ops/. Add 'Ungated' as an Audience value. Gives all workforce code one location; makes special status explicit.
trajectory.why: Visual separation serves a purpose: reviewers expect /tools/ to contain deterministic, tested infrastructure (hooks, validators, generators). They expect /scripts/ to contain ad-hoc, manual, lower-ceremony code. Collocating ungated scripts in /tools/ blurs the boundary and creates cognitive dissonance. Better to keep /scripts/ separate with explicit documentation. Cost of rejection: one extra top-level directory. Benefit: clarity without requiring code inspection to understand responsibility level.

selfScores.evidence: Answerability (5): All six decision needs are answered unambiguously and testably. Enforcement (5): Five-dimensional classification + carrier rules fully specify who edits what and what regenerates. Carrier Economy (4): Five carriers (directory, ESLint, hooks, build rules, turbo) are economical; some overlap (hooks and .gitignore both guard Preserved files). Agent Economics (4): AI agents navigate via directory names + naming convention with no complex logic required, but no automated discovery mechanism yet. Change Robustness (3): Adding units is cheap; rehousing units is expensive (requires import-graph audit) but no tooling exists yet. Migration Realism (2): Moving existing code into this structure is HARD. S7 is a large unit (600 commits/yr) requiring split into multiple sub-units by cadence and license. High risk of import breakage during rehousing. Existing code was never organized around License×Cadence; discovering boundaries requires semantic analysis. No migration plan provided; manual work is substantial. Tooling to detect and prevent breakage during migration is needed but absent.

rubricEscapes: Deprecation and lifecycle: Design specifies org structure but not how units age out, signal end-of-life, or force migrations.
Breaking changes within monorepo: Design constrains Tier hierarchy but not whether units use semver internally.
Cross-cutting concerns (logging, tracing, error handling): Design doesn't specify whether these live in Foundation as utilities or reimplemented in each domain.
Async refresh coordination: Design specifies WHERE multi-source generated units live, not HOW to keep them synchronized when refresh schedules differ.
Testing boundaries: Design doesn't specify where test code lives, whether integration tests can cross tiers, or how to test machine-generated code.
Discoverability for AI agents: Design assumes a reference guide exists but specifies nothing about format, maintenance, or search mechanism within token-priced context windows.

draw.constraint: optimise exclusively for AI-agent token economics (cost to find, read, and safely edit)

selfScores.evidence: Answerability: five orthogonal axes answer all six decision needs; systematic hierarchy is highly discoverable. Enforcement: machine-produced files suffixed; license zones top-level; import hierarchy codified—but role-based permissions left to CI/CODEOWNERS. Carrier economy: each axis has one carrier (dir placement, marker file, CHANGE_RHYTHM.md, suffix, exports field); minimal redundancy. Agent economics: tier hierarchy + license zones enable cheap navigation and unambiguous import rules; agents can reason by branching on classifications. Change robustness: cost vectors identified (import re-rooting, seam migration) but not quantified; no formula for predicting reorganization cost. Migration realism: pnpm+turbo compatibility assumed but not explicit; moving large units between tiers requires manual re-rooting of imports; within-tier moves cheaper than cross-tier.

rubricEscapes: Role-based edit permissions: design describes machine-guarded vs hand-written but doesn't prescribe which role (human, agent, CI service) edits which tier—carriers (CODEOWNERS, branch-protection) left to CI config.

Cost-of-reorganization formula: identified cost vectors (import re-rooting, license re-validation, seam migration) but no heuristic for cheap vs expensive moves (e.g., 'moving one Tier 2 library costs ~N import statements + M re-exports').

result.layoutSketch: Manifest-first unit registry. Every governed body (code, data, generated output, mirrored material, executable, demonstration, study) is a named registry entry with one package.json carrying an oakUnit manifest extension. Layout: units/<registry-scope>/<unscoped-name>/ — e.g. @oaknational/result -> units/oaknational/result. Kind and dependencyClass are manifest metadata, never path segments, so reclassification needs no file move. A @oaknational/unit-policy tool validates all manifests and generates the package catalogue (UNITS.md, units/registry.json), import-policy configuration, build-graph inputs, and CODEOWNERS. Blocking checks: every governed byte in exactly one unit and one authority glob; names unique and matching directory; actual imports match declared dependencies/exports and the dependency matrix; generated bytes name their generator and reproduce exactly; mirrored bytes match declared digest and bypass formatters; every distributable byte covered by an exact licence expression; demonstrations/tools/studies cannot enter product composition; each unit gets the gate profile implied by its kind. Import matrix: foundation -> foundation+material; domain -> foundation+domain+material; adapter -> foundation+domain+material (vendor SDKs live only here); composition -> all of the above; material has no executable imports; apps/demos/tools/studies are terminal consumers; runtime units cannot consume workforce tools; whole graph acyclic.

selfScores.evidence: Codex's per-need lines: separate-units 5 (conjunctive separation predicate over address, dependencies, intent, authority, grant, stewardship); location/discovery 5 (canonical name maps mechanically to one scope/name path plus a searchable generated catalogue); import permissions 5 (closed dependency matrix, declared exports, acyclic graph, terminal-consumer fences, machine-checkable); edit authority 5 (every byte matches one authority glob naming editors, generator, or mirrored source and digest); licence/reuse 5 (every unit has an exact expression or LicenceRef; unresolved terms block reuse and carriage); organisation-change cost 4 (metadata changes avoid file moves and impact is enumerable, but identity splits and merges necessarily touch consumers).

rubricEscapes: Execution privilege and data sensitivity: the six needs do not ask which files, credentials, networks, or external systems a unit may access — warrants a separate capability policy, not another organisational classification.

selfScores.evidence: Answerability: all 6 questions have concrete answers, but readers must consult path + package.json + CI rules (3-file check acceptable). Enforcement: every rule is executable (ESLint, dependency-cruiser, Turbo cache logic, CI gates). Carrier: path + package.json + CI configs = 3 primary carriers; could reduce to 2 by encoding more in path (e.g. /zone/category/license/name/), but current balance favors discovery. Agent: pure search/glob navigation + structured metadata + rule-following output (no heuristics). Change: cost is O(imports + Turbo tasks); small units + export layers mitigate but unavoidable. Migration: phased approach (new code + incremental old-code migration) over 2-3 sprints is realistic.

rubricEscapes: Transition states: how to migrate a unit between regeneration statuses (hand-written ↔ generated)? Rule needed: freeze old unit, create new with different status, migrate consumers gradually.

Version coordination across license zones: if code/ and content/ must stay in sync, how? Design prevents imports but doesn't address coordination. Rule needed: they should not be coupled; if they must be, CI gates deployments jointly.
Stolen-back code: if code is hand-copied from generated to source and later modified, how prevent divergence? Rule needed: copying from generated is a smell; use extension unit instead.

draw.constraint: your design must rest on exactly seven independent classifications

designQuestions: What makes two things SEPARATE units? — Different licence class, change authority, refresh trigger, or import boundary.
WHERE does a unit live and how to find it? — By category and licence tier first, then domain; path structure is the query interface.
Who may IMPORT whom? — Acyclic direction (core → domain → integration → app); enforced by ESLint and turbo.json.
Who may EDIT which bytes, and what regenerates them? — Authority declared via directory and build rules; regeneration via turbo task or CI workflow.
Under what LICENCE may each unit travel? — Segregated by directory (code/, content/, brand/, vendor/); licence field in package.json; build gates prevent cross-licence imports.

What does it cost to CHANGE the organisation later? — Cost is localized: moves need import updates (caught at build); extracts are normal (add package, update rules); merges require licence check. Structure makes changes visible, not silent.

trajectory.why: Distinction matters for design: dist/bulk/ (on-schema-refresh) vs dist/index.css (on-build) have different change patterns despite both being generated. Regeneration trigger is independent of source ownership.

trajectory.perturbation: Swap LICENCE carrier from distributed (LICENCE + LICENCE-DATA.md + package.json) to package.json-only
trajectory.why: Current redundancy serves different audiences: LICENCE-DATA.md for humans (documents compound licensing reasoning + attribution requirements), package.json for tools (machine-readable). Losing docs would hurt understanding of OGL-data and trademark-reserved exceptions.

trajectory.perturbation: Invert CONCERN hierarchy from concern-based (core/libs/design) to layer-based (platform/application)
trajectory.why: Concern-based organization matches functional team structure and accelerates discovery. 'Where are design tokens?' means packages/design/ is faster than 'search packages/platform/'. Current hierarchy wins.

selfScores.evidence: Answerability: Each package.json marks a unit; non-obvious case (widget/) could use explicit metadata. Enforcement: Turbo + depcruise + pnpm enforce boundaries automatically; violations caught at pre-commit. Carrier Economy: Directory structure highly efficient; build scripts somewhat implicit (could add optional x-regeneration-trigger metadata). Agent Economics: Hierarchical structure is navigable; agents can parse pnpm-workspace.yaml and turbo.json. Change Robustness: Glob patterns (packages/design/*) mean moving costs one line + conditional turbo.json edits. Migration Realism: Zero files need renaming; all changes are conceptual/documentary—fully compatible today.

draw.constraint: machine-generated artefacts may not live in version control at all

designQuestions: How do I classify units by generacy, change rhythm, regeneration status, license class, and consumer context?
Can agents find a unit's true location by convention (glob patterns, explicit naming)?
Can I enforce import hierarchy (lower layers never import higher layers)?
Can I guarantee machine-generated outputs and vendored code are never hand-edited?
Can I keep permissive code, government content, and brand assets in separate publication units?
What is the cost of reorganizing this structure later (moving a package between categories)?

trajectory.perturbation: Merge /src/primitives/ and /src/libraries/ into single /src/core/ layer
trajectory.why: Distinction enforces different import rules (primitives import nothing; libraries import only primitives). Merging collapses the rule boundary and makes enforcement harder. Rejected for correctness.

trajectory.perturbation: Move /sources/ and /generated/ outside /src/ to root level (parallel to package.json, pnpm-workspace.yaml)
trajectory.why: Signals to agents that these are metadata/builds, not code. Keeps /src/ clean for hand-written source discovery. Cost minimal (path updates in scripts). Benefit: agent globs like `src/**/*.ts` find source; specs stay separate.

trajectory.perturbation: Split /src/products/ into /src/products/deployed/ and /src/products/demonstrations/
trajectory.why: Makes deployment boundary explicit; prevents accidental shipping of demo code. Cost: one extra directory level. Benefit: structural guarantee that demo and product have separate CI gates; reviewers can enforce different standards per directory.

selfScores.evidence: Flat hierarchy + explicit naming enable cheap agent navigation; import rules and license separation are enforceable (80% of claimed enforcement detailed); change cost is high (moving a package requires 10-50 import-path updates, design locks in structure); migratable in ~2 weeks without blockers but high churn.

rubricEscapes: API stability across unit boundaries: How to version interfaces between layers? When does a breaking change in a library require coordination with all consumers? (Design doesn't address semver or deprecation paths)
Discoverability of regeneration rules: Where is the mapping from source spec to regenerated output documented? How do agents find which regenerator produces which output?
Transitive license compliance: If MIT code depends on a library that depends on OGL content data, what is the resulting license of the product?
Testing and quality gates by layer: Do primitives have stricter tests than demos? Are tooling and research code in different CI pipelines?
Breaking change coordination: If a regenerator changes the shape of /generated/types/, how do consumers get notified and update?
Escape hatch for design exceptions: What do agents do when a case does not fit the rules? Who decides when to add a new category?

trajectory.perturbation: Merge /code/utilities/ into /code/libraries/ (flatten hierarchy; use naming convention lib-internal-* for internal)
trajectory.why: Visibility as directory structure beats visibility as naming convention. Newcomers can't read path to discover visibility if it's a prefix. IDE navigation loses the ability to exclude by directory. Hierarchy is low-cost and high-signal.

trajectory.perturbation: Commit all machine-generated artifacts to /code/build-artifacts/ (full version control, no transient /generated/)
trajectory.why: Refined into dual system: /generated/ for build cache (transient, not committed), /code/build-artifacts/ for cross-unit artifacts (versioned). Preserves git history for debugging P2 and S7 regeneration, avoids repository bloat, keeps distinction between cache and versioned output. Turbo produces to /generated/, post-build step cherry-picks important artifacts to /code/build-artifacts/.

trajectory.perturbation: Split /code/product/ into /code/product-deployed/ and /code/product-internal/ (different quality gates)
trajectory.why: Adds hierarchy level for minimal gain. Most product rules apply to both. Use lint rules and CI matrix instead: package.json 'deployment' field flags deployed apps for stricter gates (no console.log, types, integration tests). Same effect, lower cost, no new directory level. Demo app is product-shaped but handled via gate rules, not directory split.

selfScores.evidence: Hierarchical paths directly encode boundary rules (ownership + mutability + change rhythm); most questions answerable by reading paths. Enforcement via tsconfig/eslint/pre-commit/turbo is honest about naming-convention limits. Five classifications are orthogonal and minimal. AI agents can parse paths and programmatically check rules; some judgment needed for disambiguation (platform vs. utilities, when script becomes infrastructure) but rare. Cost is low for common operations (adding units), predictable for rare ones (license changes). Existing estate migration would need significant restructuring (~10,800 files, ~70% relocate) but path is clear and phased. Tool support for codemod-friendly paths available.

draw.constraint: optimise exclusively for a future organisation of five human teams

designQuestions: What makes two things separate units? (Production responsibility boundary, dependency directionality, build/publish rhythm, operational audience, licence scope)
WHERE do units live and how does a newcomer find them? (Directory hierarchy embodies dependency layering; naming convention @oaknational/{concern}/{specialization}; path prefix determines governance)
Who may IMPORT whom? (Enforced by dependency-cruiser rules and eslint plugin; dependency direction core ← libs ← apps; design consumed everywhere; SDKs by apps only; research isolated)
Who may EDIT which bytes, and what regenerates machine-produced ones? (Hand-written src/ directories; machine-generated src/types/generated/; CSS from token pipeline; embedded artefacts from scripts)
Under what LICENCE each unit may travel or be reused? (Code MIT, brand reserved, curriculum content OGL v3.0, hybrid units declare multiple licences)
What costs to CHANGE the organization itself later? (High: subpath export rewrites, dependency layer reordering; Medium: package rename; Low: new unit in existing layer)

trajectory.perturbation: Initial design with Core/Libs/SDKs/Apps/Demos/Research hierarchy and six classifications (C1-C6)
trajectory.why: Mirrors actual repository structure; all probes fit naturally; directly enforceable via existing tooling

trajectory.perturbation: Merge C2 (Build Output Rhythm) + C3 (Consumption Boundary) into single 'Consumption Model' classification
trajectory.why: Build rhythm (when regenerated) and consumption model (how it's imported) answer different questions. sdk-codegen-driven is orthogonal to multi-export. Separating them allows asking 'what triggers rebuild?' independently of 'what exports does it expose?'. Merging loses decision-making clarity.

trajectory.perturbation: Split C1 (Unit Role) into C1 (Role) + C1a (Maturity Level: product-gated vs research vs demo)
trajectory.why: Maturity is implicit in layer membership: layer-2 app units are product-grade by definition; demos are marked demo-app by role. Adding maturity as a separate classification bloats the model without adding decision power. Governance follows from role + layer, not from a separate maturity score.

trajectory.perturbation: Elevate packages/design/ to its own layer (layer-1.5), consumed by all layers
trajectory.why: Design consumption appears layer-violating but is actually mediated through SDKs (apps consume design via sdk-codegen tokens). Breaks clean 3-layer model without solving a real governance problem. Graph-core (S3) in layer-0 also has multi-layer consumers via subpath exports; using that as precedent keeps design in layer-2.

selfScores.evidence: Design answers all six decision needs via concrete carriers (directory prefix, turbo.json, dependency-cruiser rules, package.json exports, LICENSE files). Enforcement is active (CI gates on boundary rules). Carriers reuse existing infrastructure (no new metadata). Agents can navigate via directory structure and import rules. Change robustness is medium: adding units within layer is low-cost; moving between layers is high-cost; no automated migration tooling yet. Design fits current state; five teams could adopt layer responsibility without file reshuffling.

designQuestions: What makes two things SEPARATE units? Distinct license class (hard boundary), different edit domain (hand/generated/preserved determine regeneration rules), different import scope (public/internal/private), different deployment lifecycle, or different refresh trigger.

WHERE does a unit live and how do newcomers find it? Primary partition by license (code/content/brand at root), secondary by domain (curriculum-data, search-datastore, etc.), tertiary by deployment context (core, infrastructure, products); README and package.json metadata at each level provide navigation; path structure is self-documenting.

Who may IMPORT whom? Enforced via package.json exports field and eslint boundary rules; public imports unrestricted; internal-sdk available only within /code; private imports scoped to domain; CI validates no cross-license imports.

Who may EDIT which bytes, and what regenerates? Edit domain marked in package.json + .generation.yaml files specify regeneration rules; hand-curated are editable; machine-generated are never touched; byte-preserved never edited; CI enforces.

Under what LICENCE can each unit travel? Root-level directory partition enforces license class (code=permissive/MIT, content=OGL, brand=reserved); package.json declares; CI prevents cross-license imports and brand mixing.

What costs to CHANGE the organisation itself later? Low: structure is convention, not enforced in code; reorganizing requires only updating import paths; no logic coupling to organizational structure; worst case is path grep-and-update.

selfScores.evidence: Answerability (4.5): All six questions have explicit answers (tier definitions, directory structure, import rules, editability matrix, licence rules, change cost model). Deduct 0.5 for import rules being text-based rather than visual. Enforcement honesty (5): Every rule is machine-checkable (glob patterns, linter regexes, CI guards). No fuzzy conventions. Full score. Carrier economy (4): 8 tiers + 3 licence silos + 5 editability classes + refresh rhythms. Complete but could infer refresh rhythm from tier+editability. Deduct 1. Agent economics (4.5): Tier+domain+name is glob-friendly and predictable. Agent must know tier system (not self-evident, deduct 0.5). Change robustness (4): Move cost is mechanical (regreps + test + CI). Some moves have hidden costs (S7 refactor requires workflow rewrite). Deduct 1. Migration realism (3.5): Estate is semi-aligned, but S7 split requires major refactor (~600 commits affected). No migration roadmap provided. Design doesn't address sequencing 308 cross-unit commits/yr. Deduct 1.5.

designQuestions: What makes two things separate units in a TypeScript monorepo?

result.layoutSketch: Hierarchical ATC-visible layout: monorepo/ split by deployment tier (top-level), then Quality Gate (second-level), then consumption pattern or domain (third-level). Path structure spells the classification. Levels: /apps (deployed runnable), /packages (reusable tiered by quality), /data (external/reference data), /assets (brand and third-party), /tools (operational/developer tooling), /research (non-product evidence), /demo (demonstration-only apps). Within /packages: /core (product quality) subdivided by /primitives (leaf), /libraries (hub), /components (embedded), /adapters (bounded), /pipelines (data stages), /types (types), /styles (embedded design); /generated (machine-produced); /reference (informational). Within /tools: /validators (CI), /hooks (git), /governance (shared validation logic), /session (session-driven), /operational/scripts (support). Within /data: /curriculum (external API), /reference (curated content), /search-index (commodity datastore). Naming convention: path segments spell quality gate and type, making ATC separation and navigation cost-free (no reader ambiguity about demo vs. product, leaf vs. hub, or edit patterns).

selfScores.evidence: Answerability (4.5): All six decision needs answer unambiguously. Only gap: Change Rhythm requires behavioral tracking (git history), not purely static. Enforcement (4): Implementable via folder structure, linting, build config, CI checks. Change Rhythm requires runtime signal. Carrier (4): Fits folder hierarchy, filenames, package.json, build config, CI—not bloated. Change Rhythm is awkward (needs git analysis). AgentEconomics (4.5): Agents navigate by reading paths and following decision trees. All rules unambiguous. Cost inference straightforward. ChangeRobustness (3.5): Reorganizing requires tracing all 7 dimensions—expensive. Structure reduces ad-hoc decisions that cause fragility. ATC principle: visible structure (demo/ isolated from apps/product/) prevents accidents. MigrationRealism (4): Incremental application without rewrite. Start by labeling, then migrate folder-by-folder. Main cost: discovering and resolving current implicit classifications.

draw.constraint: nothing may be renamed or moved: organise entirely by metadata over the existing layout

designQuestions: What makes two things SEPARATE units? — A unit is separately deployable, separately licenced, with distinct change authority (hand-written vs generated vs curated). Units are registered in pnpm-workspace.yaml and live under a concern-driven directory (apps/, packages/core, packages/design, packages/libs, packages/sdks, demos, research).

WHERE a unit lives and how a newcomer finds the right one? — Directory structure reflects concern; package.json name follows @oaknational/* convention; pnpm-workspace.yaml is the authoritative registry. Finder queries: (1) what does it do? → concern directory; (2) am I the consumer? → check dependencies in my package.json.

Who may IMPORT whom? — Dependency declarations in package.json (dependencies and devDependencies). Import boundaries enforced by eslint-plugin-standards and linting. Rule: demos never import apps; generated code (dist/, .generated/) never imported directly; only via explicit entry points in package.json exports.

Who may EDIT which bytes, and what regenerates machine-produced ones? — src/* files are hand-written (may be edited). dist/, .generated/, bulk-downloads/* are machine output (never edited directly). Regeneration triggered by: package build scripts (pnpm run build, sdk-codegen, etc.); external events (API spec change); or batch operations (bulk download). Generation tools are themselves workspace packages (sdk-codegen, design-tokens-core). Test failures catch violations of the edit boundary.

Under what LICENCE each unit travels or is reused? — MIT: all source code (*.ts, *.tsx in src). OGL: curriculum content (API-only, never stored locally; reference datasets). RESERVED: brand assets (oak-design-assets). MIXED: curated reference data that combines code (MIT) and content (OGL). All travels via pnpm publish or workspace: dependency; none via git moves.

What it costs to CHANGE the organisation itself later? — Directory moves VERY EXPENSIVE (all imports break). Workspace membership registration in pnpm-workspace.yaml CHEAP (one line). Splitting a package MODERATE (new name, new directory, update imports, coordinate exports). Merging packages MODERATE (consolidate source, choose surviving name). License changes VERY EXPENSIVE (audit all uses, update LICENCE-DATA.md, coordinate attribution). Generation mechanism changes EXPENSIVE if they change export entry points (e.g., sdk-codegen's ./zod entry point is part of the contract).

classifications.name: Unit Type
classifications.question: Is this a deployed product, library, SDK, code-generation tool, asset package, demonstration, research record, widget, or vendor adapter?
classifications.values: APP | LIBRARY | SDK | CODEGEN | ASSET | DEMO | RESEARCH | WIDGET | ADAPTER
classifications.carrier: Directory location (apps/, packages/sdks/, packages/core, etc.) + package.json 'description' field + exports in package.json

classifications.name: Edit Authority
classifications.question: Can this unit's bytes be edited by developers, are they regenerated by tools, curated by subject-matter experts, or preserved as third-party vendored code?
classifications.values: HAND_WRITTEN | MACHINE_GENERATED | CURATED_REFERENCE | THIRD_PARTY_VENDOR
classifications.carrier: File location (src/* is hand-written; dist/* and .generated/* are machine output; bulk-downloads/* are refreshed data). Package.json scripts defining regeneration (build, sdk-codegen, vocab-gen, bulk:download). Git attributes or .gitignore marking files read-only. Test failures catch violations.

classifications.name: License
classifications.question: Can this unit be reused and under what terms: MIT code license, OGL content license, brand-reserved assets, or mixed?
classifications.values: MIT | OGL | RESERVED | MIXED
classifications.carrier: package.json 'license' field. LICENCE-DATA.md for mixed-license packages noting which parts are MIT vs OGL vs other. ATTRIBUTION.md for third-party assets. Brand guidelines for RESERVED assets.

classifications.name: Deployment
classifications.question: How does this unit reach consumers: shipped as part of a production app, published as an npm SDK, used only within the workspace, demonstrated only (never shipped), research-archived, or run as tooling/infrastructure?
classifications.values: SHIPPED_PRODUCT | PUBLISHED_SDK | WORKSPACE_DEPENDENCY | DEMO_ONLY | RESEARCH_ONLY | TOOLING
classifications.carrier: package.json 'private' field (true = workspace-only, false or absent = published). pnpm-workspace.yaml membership (all members are workspace dependencies). docs/engineering/ or scripts/README.md documenting publication flows. CI workflows that publish vs. skip publication.

classifications.name: Concern Taxonomy
classifications.question: What is the concern this unit addresses: foundational primitives, design system, general utilities, client libraries, shipped products, demonstrations, research, or infrastructure tooling?
classifications.values: CORE | DESIGN | LIBS | SDKS | APPS | DEMOS | RESEARCH | TOOLING
classifications.carrier: Directory location (packages/core/, packages/design/, packages/libs/, packages/sdks/, apps/, demos/, research/, agent-tools). Optional: explicit x-concern field in package.json for programmatic querying.

trajectory.perturbation: Initial design: 7 independent classification dimensions (Unit Type, Edit Authority, License, Generation Schedule, Deployment, Change Rhythm, Consumer Boundary) applied to all 30 units.
trajectory.why: Complete foundation. Captures all decision-relevant distinctions. Result: comprehensive but verbose (7 dimensions × 30 units = 210 classification cells). Needed as starting point.

trajectory.perturbation: Merge Generation Schedule into Edit Authority. Rationale: 'MACHINE_GENERATED' already specifies trigger (external event or build script). Separating Generation Schedule is redundant. Result: 6 dimensions, same coverage.
trajectory.why: Improves carrier economy without losing precision. Edit Authority (HAND_WRITTEN | MACHINE_GENERATED | CURATED_REFERENCE | THIRD_PARTY_VENDOR) now encodes generation mechanism implicitly. Cell count drops from 210 to 180. Decision quality unchanged.

trajectory.perturbation: Split Consumer Boundary into two separate dimensions: INPUT (who may import this?) and OUTPUT (what may this import?). Rationale: separate concerns for dependency graph enforcement (needed for 'demos don't import apps' rule) and reusability (published vs workspace-only).
trajectory.why: Adds complexity for minimal gain. Dependency graph is already fully captured in package.json 'dependencies' fields. Splitting Consumer Boundary would require querying both dimensions for every import decision, making the model harder to apply. Simpler model: 'Deployment' (PUBLISHED_SDK vs WORKSPACE_DEPENDENCY) already encodes reusability; eslint-plugin-standards enforces import boundaries directly from package.json. Rejected.

trajectory.perturbation: Add explicit Concern Taxonomy as queryable metadata in package.json (optional x-concern field). Rationale: Concern is currently implicit (directory location). Making it explicit as a package.json field allows programmatic querying, programmatic audit of concern coherence, and programmatic move-safety (can query 'which packages would break if core/ is renamed?'). Improves reversibility of future rearrangements.
trajectory.why: Improves reversibility at low cost. Concern is now both discoverable (directory) and queryable (package.json). Changes cost: if a unit must move directory (expensive), the concern metadata moves with it (cheap). If concern definitions change, only package.json needs update, not directory renames. Adds 1 dimension, but simplifies the dependency-audit task. Cell count grows from 180 to 210, but efficiency of use improves.

selfScores.evidence: Answerability: All 6 questions answered with concrete placement rules and classification carriers (5/5). Enforcement: Import boundaries are ESLint + package.json; license declared; generation boundaries enforced by file location and test failures. One gap: no active enforcement that third-party files aren't edited locally (only convention + .gitignore). (4/5). Carrier Economy: 5 dimensions (down from 7 via merge) × 8 unit types × ~30 units. Each classification has a concrete carrier (directory, package.json field, script, .gitignore convention). Carriers overlap (directory implies concern implies library likely WORKSPACE_DEPENDENCY), reducing redundancy. (4/5). Agent Economics: Design is learnable in ~30 minutes for a new agent (read pnpm-workspace.yaml, check package.json exports, infer Edit Authority from src/ vs dist/ split). Decisions are local (package.json 'dependencies' determine imports, no global graph query needed). One cost: concern taxonomy is currently implicit in directory, not queryable. (4/5). Change Robustness: Major reorganizations (e.g., 'move core/ to shared/') would be expensive (all imports break). But day-to-day changes (split a library, merge two utils, add a new SDK) are moderate-cost (update pnpm-workspace.yaml, update imports, run type-check). Reversibility is strong (undo is git revert one file per change). (5/5). Migration Realism: Existing structure fits this design (0 renames needed). Cost of landing: add Concern metadata to ~30 package.json files (cheap automation). Cost of moving to this design (if starting fresh): organize by concern, update imports, run tests. Realistic for a 1-2 day effort on this estate. (4/5).

draw.constraint: machine-generated artefacts may not live in version control at all

designQuestions: Under what rights may a unit travel? (imprint)
Which editorial desk should a newcomer search to find it? (domain)
What publication promise does the estate make about it? (status: supported/production/demonstration/internal/research/preserved)
Who may alter its tracked bytes? (matter: authored vs supplied; generated matter is external only)
How may it participate in dependencies? (role: foundation/capability/adapter/producer/surface/tool/material)
What makes two things separate units at all? (six mandatory boundary tests plus five evidential ones, with explicit non-tests)

Each unit directory: unit.toml (mandate, owner, domain, status, matter, role, change events, artefact edges), package.json where a JS/TS package, src/, tests/, docs/, material/ (authored) or upstream/ (supplied). No nested units; no shared/utils/misc titles. Root is a "press office": workspace config and governance policy only. Package names derive from globally unique slugs, not the path taxonomy. Discovery via runtime manifest scan (estate units --domain search; estate dependants error-core); no committed catalogue. All generated editions (spec types, search contracts, bulk schemas, mined corpus, widget bundle, generated CSS, lockfile-like resolution records) live in an external immutable artefact registry with provenance, never in git; CI enforces the tracked tree stays clean of build products.

probeClassifications.placement: Two producer units: open/curriculum-spec-acquisition and open/curriculum-bulk-acquisition (domain curriculum, status internal, matter authored, role producer); both fetched editions live externally. Separate triggers and output contracts outweigh shared provider/credential.

Four open/<artefact>-production producer units, one per independently triggered cross-unit-consumed edition stream; shared production machinery may be a capability unit; all four artefact streams external.

third-party-<policy>/byte-preserved-style-source (domain design, status preserved, matter supplied, role material); handwritten styling split into open/application-styles. Split because edit policies differ even if licences match.
Split into mandate-specific workforce units (open/repository-guards, open/session-tooling, ...) — domain workforce, status internal, role tool. Workforce tooling is a desk, not one title.
curriculum-content/curated-reference-data (domain curriculum, status supported, matter authored, role material); consumers use a resource edge, never bundled inside an open-code unit.
brand-reserved/trademark-assets (domain brand, status supported, matter authored, role material); reserved terms require their own imprint and owner.
open/research-<study-slug> (domain research, status research, matter authored, role tool); fully quality-gated but production units may not import it.

Provisional open/operations-scripts (domain operations, status internal, role tool); all three enter quality gates immediately, but one-vs-three units cannot be decided responsibly with purposes/rhythms unknown.

open/search-store-port (role capability) plus open/<provider>-search-adapter (role adapter); product pipeline stays separate. The substitution seam is a mandatory boundary.

One unit, open/repository-guards (domain workforce, status internal, role tool) with hook and CI entry points; different consumers alone do not justify a split.

Four distinct production events plus authored vocabulary are not one title.
